# MIPS32 big endian: snippets that need labels.
#
# ---- Why every snippet ends with `.p2align 6` ----
#
# rsasm always assembles as `.set noreorder`: what is written is what is
# emitted. llvm-mc defaults to `.set reorder`, where it appends a `nop` to fill
# the delay slot of every branch and jump, making its output one word longer.
# rsasm's core `.set` directive does not yet accept GNU as's MIPS options, so
# `.set noreorder` cannot simply be written at the top of the file.
#
# The padding absorbs the difference: MIPS `nop` is the all-zero word, and so
# is alignment fill, so once both outputs are rounded up to the same multiple
# of 64 they are byte-identical -- and the branch word itself, which is the
# thing under test, is still compared.
#
# This only works when the extra word cannot move anything the branch measures
# against, so every snippet branches *backwards* to a label at its top and puts
# the branch last.

=== beq backward
foo:
beq $1, $2, foo
.p2align 6

=== beq across two instructions
foo:
addiu $4, $4, 1
addiu $5, $5, -1
beq $4, $5, foo
.p2align 6

=== bne
foo:
bne $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== blez
foo:
blez $a0, foo
.p2align 6

=== bgtz
foo:
bgtz $a0, foo
.p2align 6

=== bltz
foo:
bltz $a0, foo
.p2align 6

=== bgez
foo:
bgez $a0, foo
.p2align 6

=== bltzal
foo:
bltzal $a0, foo
.p2align 6

=== bgezal
foo:
bgezal $a0, foo
.p2align 6

=== b
foo:
b foo
.p2align 6

=== bal
foo:
bal foo
.p2align 6

=== beqz
foo:
beqz $v0, foo
.p2align 6

=== bnez
foo:
bnez $v0, foo
.p2align 6

=== bge
foo:
bge $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== bgt
foo:
bgt $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== ble
foo:
ble $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== blt
foo:
blt $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== bgeu
foo:
bgeu $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== bgtu
foo:
bgtu $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== bleu
foo:
bleu $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== bltu
foo:
bltu $a0, $a1, foo
.p2align 6

=== bge against zero folds to bgez
foo:
bge $a0, $zero, foo
.p2align 6

=== blt against zero folds to bltz
foo:
blt $a0, $zero, foo
.p2align 6

=== jr
foo:
jr $ra
.p2align 6

=== jalr one operand links through ra
foo:
jalr $t9
.p2align 6

=== jalr two operands
foo:
jalr $s0, $t9
.p2align 6

=== bc1f
foo:
bc1f foo
.p2align 6

=== bc1t
foo:
bc1t foo
.p2align 6

=== a backwards loop
loop:
lw $t0, 0($a0)
addiu $a0, $a0, 4
addiu $a1, $a1, -1
sw $t0, 0($a1)
bnez $a1, loop
.p2align 6

# A forward branch would normally be thrown off by llvm-mc's inserted delay
# slot, since the extra word sits between the branch and its target. Aligning
# the target absorbs that word too, so the measured distance stays the same.
=== beq forward over an alignment
beq $1, $2, end
.p2align 6
end:
nop

=== bnez forward over an alignment
bnez $a0, end
.p2align 6
end:
nop

=== j
foo:
j foo
.p2align 6

=== jal
foo:
jal foo
.p2align 6

# Unresolved references leave their field zero and emit a relocation, so the
# .text bytes are comparable even though the addresses are not yet known.
=== la of an external symbol
la $a0, extern_sym
nop

=== explicit hi and lo halves
lui $a0, %hi(extern_sym)
addiu $a0, $a0, %lo(extern_sym)
lw $a1, %lo(extern_sym)($a0)
nop

=== hi and lo of a local symbol
sym = 0x12345678
lui $a0, %hi(sym)
addiu $a0, $a0, %lo(sym)
nop

=== hi and lo where the low half is negative
sym = 0x1234abcd
lui $a0, %hi(sym)
addiu $a0, $a0, %lo(sym)
nop

# `j` takes an absolute address, so a number means the same thing to both
# assemblers here (unlike a conditional branch, where llvm-mc reads a bare
# number as the displacement). The top four bits come from the PC, so a target
# above 256 MB is not out of range.
=== j to an absolute address
j 0x400000
.p2align 6

=== jal into kseg0
jal 0x80001000
.p2align 6

=== j to the last word of a region
j 0x0ffffffc
.p2align 6
